facts.text: On this date in 1783, the Treaty of Paris was signed, officially ending the American Revolutionary War — nearly two years after the fighting had stopped.
On September 3, 1967, Sweden switched overnight from driving on the left to the right. The government had prepared for years; accidents actually dropped sharply in the weeks that followed.
More people live inside a circle drawn around Manila than inside one drawn around New York City of the same radius — Southeast Asia's density defies almost any Western intuition.
Canada has more lakes than every other country on Earth combined, holding roughly 60% of the world's total freshwater lake surface area.
Vatican City's population is overwhelmingly male and middle-aged, making it statistically the world's least demographically normal sovereign state — no births are recorded there most years.
On this day in 1929, the Dow Jones peaked at 381 points — a level it would not reclaim for 25 years, not until November 1954.
On September 3, 1658, Oliver Cromwell died, triggering a political crisis that within two years restored the monarchy and reshaped England's financial system entirely.
The Dutch East India Company, history's first publicly traded corporation, at its 1637 peak held a market cap equivalent to roughly $8 trillion in today's dollars.
Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway originally made textiles. He later called buying it the worst investment of his life, costing him an estimated $200 billion in opportunity cost.
The entire global bond market — around $130 trillion — is larger than global equity markets, yet receives a fraction of the financial press coverage stocks do.
On this date in 1976, Viking 2 landed on Mars. The soil samples it collected were so chemically reactive that scientists spent decades debating whether they had accidentally detected life.
On this date in 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed mold killing bacteria in a petri dish he had left out before a vacation — the sloppiest experiment in history became penicillin.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A single teaspoon of its matter would weigh about a billion tons on Earth.
Your body contains roughly 37 trillion cells, but you host about 38 trillion bacterial cells. You are, by count, slightly more microbe than human.
Light from the Sun takes 8 minutes to reach Earth, but took around 100,000 years to travel from the Sun's core to its surface before that.
On this day in 1189, Richard I was crowned King of England — a man who ruled England for a decade and spent roughly six months of it there.
On this day in 1939, Britain declared war on Germany. The BBC interrupted its programming, then resumed a Donald Duck cartoon.
The fax machine was invented in 1843, twenty-one years before anyone had laid a transcontinental railroad.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid — by over 900 years.
The University of Oxford was already 300 years old when the Aztec Empire was founded.
Sonder (n.): the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in *The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows*, 2012. Too precise to stay obscure for long.
Hiraeth (n.): a Welsh longing for a home that may never have existed — grief, nostalgia, and yearning fused into one syllable the English language simply cannot replicate.

On this date in 1658, Oliver Cromwell died, and England exhaled. The old Norse word *cromwellian* never caught on, but *interregnum* — Latin for 'between reigns' — entered common English precisely to describe the hollow years his rule created.

Mamihlapinatapai: a Yaghan word from Tierra del Fuego describing a look shared by two people who both want something but won't be the first to say so. Listed in the Guinness Book as the world's most succinct word.

On this date in 1939, Britain declared war on Germany. The word *blitz* entered English within months — borrowed from German *Blitzkrieg* (lightning war), then clipped by Londoners into something almost casual, the way language tames what terror cannot.
On this date in 2017, China's central bank declared ICOs illegal and ordered all completed token sales to refund investors — erasing roughly $60B in crypto market cap within 72 hours.
On this date in 2012, Satoshi's final known email to Gavin Andresen was sent, signing off with 'I've moved on to other things' — the last verifiable communication from Bitcoin's creator.
Bitcoin's genesis block contains an unspendable 50 BTC reward. Satoshi hardcoded it that way: the coinbase transaction references no prior output, making the coins permanently unclaimable by design.
Ethereum's gas limit is not fixed in the protocol — it's a rolling average adjusted block-by-block via miner (now validator) votes, meaning block capacity is set by consensus, not code.
The 2016 DAO hack didn't steal funds — it legally withdrew them under the contract's own rules. The Ethereum community forked not because the code failed, but because it worked exactly as written.

On this date in 2019, OpenAI released GPT-2 in full after a staged rollout it had delayed over misuse fears — the first time a lab publicly rationed a model release, a practice that quietly became industry norm.
On this date in 2024, Google DeepMind's AlphaProof solved four of six problems from the International Mathematical Olympiad, crossing a threshold most researchers had placed a decade away.
The training run for GPT-4 is estimated to have consumed roughly 50 gigawatt-hours of electricity — comparable to the annual residential consumption of about 4,600 US homes.

RLHF, the technique that made large language models conversationally coherent, was first described in a 2017 paper with 'Atari' in the title; its authors had no idea it would become the alignment method of record.

Transformers were introduced in 2017 specifically to replace recurrence in sequence modeling — the authors expected the architecture to remain a niche NLP tool, not become the substrate for nearly every frontier model across vision, audio, and protein folding.
